title: The Evening Brief: Courts block Trump on Carroll, FBI, and Disney; new suits test First Amendment limits
dek: Federal courts have now constrained the Trump administration on three fronts in a single day: the Supreme Court finalized a $5 million judgment against Trump in the Carroll case, a judge blocked his attempt to relocate the FBI headquarters, and Disney sued the FCC alleging retaliation for broadcast content. Meanwhile, new legal disputes over speech protections have emerged.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: The day's litigation pattern reveals courts willing to enforce statutory limits and prior decisions against executive action, while several First Amendment questions, on government investigation of political speech, regulatory pressure on broadcasters, and interstate extradition, remain unresolved and headed for adjudication.
bottom_line: Three federal courts tightened constraints on Trump administration actions today: the Supreme Court finalized the $5 million Carroll verdict, a judge blocked the FBI headquarters relocation reversal, and Disney challenged what it alleges is FCC retaliation for editorial content. Simultaneously, new First Amendment cases surfaced, a DHS investigation of political speech, an extradition standoff, and a campus shooting with documented digital evidence, positioning courts to weigh the boundaries of government power over speech, regulatory authority, and interstate cooperation in coming weeks. The Carroll $83 million appeal and the Disney restraining order decision remain critical checkpoints.
body: Three federal rulings today constrained Trump administration actions, while new First Amendment cases widened the legal landscape. The Supreme Court declined for a second time to hear Trump's appeal of the $5 million E. Jean Carroll verdict, making that judgment final and unreviewable. Trump has already paid the full amount plus interest, totaling $5.62 million as of this summer. A separate $83 million verdict from a 2024 trial remains in the appeals process. U.S. District Judge Theodore D. Chuang blocked the Trump administration's plan to move FBI headquarters from a Maryland site to the Ronald Reagan Building in Washington, finding the decision exceeded statutory authority and that Congress had previously limited the agency's choice to three specific locations, none of which was the Reagan Building. The judge also determined that the FBI's decision to redirect previously appropriated funds toward the move was arbitrary and capricious.

Disney and ABC filed suit on August 18 against the Federal Communications Commission, challenging an order requiring eight Disney-owned ABC television stations to file broadcast license renewal applications years ahead of schedule. The company sought a temporary restraining order and characterized the renewal demand as an "existential threat." The licenses were not due for renewal until 2028 at the earliest. Disney alleged the FCC order was retaliation for the network's editorial decisions, while the FCC disputes that claim and cited ongoing investigations into Disney's diversity practices and The View program's compliance with public interest standards. The case raises core First Amendment questions about regulatory pressure on press freedom.

A separate First Amendment dispute emerged from a Department of Homeland Security investigation. Federal ICE agents tracked David Streever, a Rochester, New York man, to his home, an airport, and a hotel to question him about an email he sent in January criticizing ICE's former acting director Todd Lyons using harsh language. ICE left Streever with a warning notice citing federal law against threatening officials. The Department of Homeland Security defended the investigation in court filings as lawful preventative action. Streever has sued, arguing the government violated his First Amendment rights. A federal judge will weigh whether warning notices and in-person confrontations about acknowledged protected speech violate the First Amendment, even if motivated by legitimate safety concerns.

Additional litigation also emerged from law enforcement conduct. Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison filed a federal lawsuit against Texas Governor Greg Abbott to compel the extradition of ICE agent Christian Castro, charged with assault with a deadly weapon and falsely reporting a crime. Castro was arrested in Texas in May after allegedly shooting a Venezuelan man in Minneapolis on January 14. A Hennepin County District Court judge found probable cause and issued a nationwide warrant; a Cameron County judge ordered Castro detained pending extradition. The suit will test whether Abbott's office offers a legal basis for withholding the warrant or whether it stands as a bare refusal to comply with interstate extradition requirements.

In Virginia, court documents revealed that Camron Harris, 19, alleged to have opened fire at Virginia State University early Saturday morning, sent Instagram messages discussing acquiring a firearm and carrying out the shooting in real time. Police were called around 1:30 a.m. for reports of gunfire. The shooting critically injured a 21-year-old man and left four others with non-life-threatening injuries. Harris faces multiple felony charges and remains in custody.
